title: Football Legend Kevin Keegan Dies at 75 After Battle With Cancer
excerpt: The two-time Ballon d'Or winner and former England captain, who revealed stage four cancer in June, was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.
body:
• Kevin Keegan, one of English football's greatest and most charismatic figures, has died at 75 after a battle with cancer.
  • He won the Ballon d'Or in 1978 and 1979 — the only Englishman to win it twice — and starred for Liverpool, Hamburg, Newcastle, and Southampton.
  • As a manager, he transformed Newcastle United into title contenders in the 1990s before a brief stint as England boss.
  • Keegan revealed in June that he had stage four cancer; he was surrounded by family in his final moments.

Kevin Keegan, the two-time Ballon d'Or winner who captained England and became one of football's most beloved figures both on and off the pitch, died on Monday at the age of 75. His family confirmed he had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

"It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75," his family said in a statement. "Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments."

A Glittering Career

Born in Armthorpe, South Yorkshire, Keegan rose from working-class origins through Scunthorpe United to become one of the most decorated English players of his generation. He joined Liverpool in 1971 and helped the club win three league titles, the FA Cup, two UEFA Cups, and the European Cup before making a groundbreaking move to Hamburg in 1977 — one of the first English players to join a continental club.

It was in Germany that Keegan won the Ballon d'Or in consecutive years, 1978 and 1979, remaining the only English player to claim the award more than once. He scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England between 1972 and 1982, captaining the national team 31 times.

"My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss."

— Alan Shearer

More Than a Footballer

Keegan transcended the sport in the 1970s with his celebrity status. His perm became a cultural touchstone, copied by footballers across Europe. He released a pop single, appeared in aftershave advertisements alongside heavyweight boxing champion Henry Cooper, and became a regular on television shows — a forerunner to the modern athlete-celebrity.

After retiring as a player, Keegan moved into management and revitalised Newcastle United in the early 1990s. His team, nicknamed "The Entertainers," played attacking football that captivated the country and came agonisingly close to the Premier League title in 1995–96, ultimately losing out to Manchester United. His touchline outburst — "I would love it if we beat them" — became one of football's most memorable moments.

Legacy and Tributes

Newcastle, where Keegan served two spells as both player and manager, called him "one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history." Southampton, Liverpool, and the Football Association all issued tributes.

Keegan had revealed in January that he was undergoing cancer treatment, and disclosed in June that his diagnosis was stage four. His death comes during the week following the 2026 FIFA World Cup final, casting a shadow over the global football community.

He is survived by his wife Jean and their two daughters.
